axes.model_access:
**Its model-access path is the most concrete. Defaults to the OpenAI API, and local models are officially named via the Ollama tool.**

The README writes in this order. Default OpenAI, plus several connection options, e.g. local models via the Ollama tool.

"CrewAI supports using various LLMs through a variety of connection options.
By default your agents will use the **OpenAI API** when querying the model.
However, there are several other ways to allow your agents to connect to models.
For example, you can configure your agents to use a **local model via the Ollama tool**."

The FAQ adds one more: **LM Studio** can also be connected.

**Official wording**: "Tools like Ollama and LM Studio allow seamless integration"

**This is especially valuable for this site's readers**: among the three orchestration frameworks,
for running local quantized models, only CrewAI names concrete tools at README-first-screen level.

**The full provider list is verified** (official `learn/llm-connections` page), in two classes:

- **native SDK integration, 5 vendors** — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Azure, AWS Bedrock
- **the rest fall back to LiteLLM**, installed via `uv add 'crewai[litellm]'`. The official page additionally names individually:
  Ollama, Mistral, Groq, Cohere, Hugging Face, Replicate, Together AI,
  Cloudflare Workers AI, DeepInfra, SambaNova, Nebius, NVIDIA NIMs.

  This list ends with "And many more!", pointing to the LiteLLM Providers docs for the full list

Also, **the official page states the default model verbatim**:

**Official wording**: "By default, CrewAI uses the `gpt-4o-mini` model."

It is decided by `OPENAI_MODEL_NAME`; unset means gpt-4o-mini. Two ways to switch:
pass a string identifier (`llm='claude-2'`), or use the `LLM` class with model / base_url / api_key.
The local snippet is given in full officially:

**Official example**: `LLM(model="ollama/llama3.2", base_url="http://localhost:11434")`

**Unknown: tool calling / structured output reliability after switching providers, not stated officially.**
(`learn/llm-connections` and `concepts/llms` pages checked; no cross-provider reliability comparison.)
axes.runtime:
**It is a pure library; the official line is "from prototype to production without changing frameworks."**

Install is a pip package (README Getting Started uses pip install + the crewai CLI); there is no hosted service.

"Move from experiment to production **without changing frameworks**."

**State persistence is positioned officially as "add as your system grows"**; both README quotes carry that qualifier:

"Add tools, memory, **checkpointing**, and async execution **as your system grows**"

"Add deterministic steps, human input, structured outputs, and **checkpointing as your system grows**"

That is README positioning language.

**The mechanism itself is documented in detail officially**. See the official `concepts/checkpointing` page:

- **granularity**: event-driven, default `on_events=["task_completed"]`,
  i.e. **one checkpoint per completed task**; `CheckpointConfig` can change frequency and caps

- **two storage backends**: `JsonProvider` (one file per checkpoint, default, under `./.checkpoints/`),
  `SqliteProvider` (a single SQLite database, WAL enabled, suited to high frequency)

- **switches**: `Crew` / `Flow` / `Agent` all accept `checkpoint`; children inherit parents by default,
  and can pass `False` to opt out

The granularity is "each completed task / method" — exactly the checkpoint granularity this site looks for.
axes.local_files:
**The framework itself ships no filesystem capability; file read/write comes from tools — but the tools' default boundary is clear.**

**The default boundary is verified** (official FileReadTool page). Paths passed in at runtime **must fall inside `base_dir`**.
`base_dir` defaults to the current working directory. `..` and symlinks are resolved before validation,

so they cannot be used to escape

Two exceptions:

- a `file_path` hardcoded in the constructor is a developer declaration and **may bypass that limit**, but only that one file is allowed
- opening a wider range requires an explicit `base_dir='/data'`

Two environment variables manage the escape hatch and the lockdown:

- escape hatch `CREWAI_TOOLS_ALLOW_UNSAFE_PATHS=true` — process-level.

  The official docs say it also turns off SSRF protection for all crewai-tools; not recommended

- managed worker apps lock it down with `CREWAI_TOOLS_FORCE_SAFE_PATHS=true`

There is also a set of **multimodal file inputs** (`crewai[file-processing]` extra, `Files` page, **early access**).
Images / PDFs / audio / video / text can be passed.

**Unknown: default permissions under container deployment, not stated officially.** (Files page and FileReadTool page checked.)
axes.background:
**It does not host a background.** The library provides no vendor-managed execution environment — for "keeps running after the computer shuts down",
you must run the process on your own servers / VPC. The AMP commercial side separately offers Cron scheduling.

**Flow's state management is explicit official wording.** The README describes Flow as
"event-driven workflows with **state, branching, routing**",
and the FAQ says Flow suits "detailed execution paths and **secure state management**".

**State is explicit and structured** (example code in the README's "Using Crews and Flows Together" section).

`class MarketState(BaseModel)`, with Flow[MarketState] reading and writing
`self.state.sentiment` and similar fields directly, branching on numeric thresholds of `self.state.confidence`.

**This is the "state" this site looks for**: explicit, structured, branchable.

**Persistence and cross-process recovery verified** (official `concepts/checkpointing`, `concepts/flows` pages):

- **Flow's `@persist` decorator**: officially "automatically persists all flow method states",
  default backend `SQLiteFlowPersistence`

- **resume**: `kickoff(inputs={"id": <uuid>})` — same `flow_uuid` continues the history
- **fork**: `kickoff(restore_from_state_id=<uuid>)` — new `state.id`, original history untouched
- **checkpoint restore**: crew / flow / agent checkpoints can be restored from `./.checkpoints/`;
  the `crewai checkpoint` CLI provides resume / fork
axes.tools:
**The official docs explicitly list MCP and A2A — one of its strengths.**

"Use tools, **memory, knowledge, checkpointing**, async execution,
and **MCP/A2A support** for more capable production agents."

**MCP is a core dependency, not an optional extra.** The official `lib/crewai/pyproject.toml`
`[project] dependencies` pins `mcp~=1.28.1` directly.

**A2A is the optional extra**: `a2a = ["a2a-sdk~=0.3.10", ...]`.
This matches the OpenAI Agents SDK putting `mcp>=1.19.0` in `dependencies` — a core capability.

The MCP integration surface:

- **three transports**: stdio / SSE / Streamable HTTP (one page each)
- **DSL field** `mcps=`; multi-server aggregation via `MCPServerAdapter`
- there is also an MCP security dedicated page
- **built-in tools** are `crewai-tools` (officially a 75+ OSS catalog, install `crewai[tools]`)

Additionally, CrewAI hosts its own documentation MCP server (`docs.crewai.com/mcp`),
queryable by AI coding assistants for its API details (the `ask-docs` mentioned in the README's "Build with AI" section).

**The A2A (Agent-to-Agent) specification and ecosystem remain an external protocol**: this site only records
**"the official docs have an `a2a` extra and a batch of A2A events"**; the protocol spec is outside this site's research scope.
axes.context:
**It provides a unified memory system plus separate knowledge. The mechanism is verified.**

Two memory-related statements in the README:

- Key Features' "memory, **knowledge**, checkpointing"
- the agent-config checklist in the "Build with AI" section:
  "Configuring agents — role, goal, backstory, tools, LLMs, **memory**, guardrails"

**The mechanism is verified, and it overturns the old judgment** (official `concepts/memory` page). The official docs now have a **unified `Memory` class**.

**Official wording**: "a single `Memory` class that replaces separate short-term, long-term,
entity, and external memory types with one intelligent API"

That is, **the old entry's "official docs do not distinguish working / long-term memory" is outdated**.

The concrete mechanism:

- **scopes**: a hierarchical scope tree (filesystem-like, e.g. `/agent/researcher`). Crew-level is shared by default.
  Agents can take a private subtree via `memory.scope("/agent/x")`. `slice()` provides cross-branch read-only / read-write views.

- **storage backend**: a vector store under the platform directory, ChromaDB by default, path changeable via `CREWAI_STORAGE_DIR`.

  The knowledge store officially "uses the same storage system as memory"

- **pruning is not simple truncation**: retrieval uses a composite `semantic + recency + importance` score.
  Writes go through LLM extraction of atomic facts + consolidation/dedup
  (when similarity crosses the threshold, the LLM decides keep / update / delete)

- **knowledge vs memory**: knowledge is a RAG fact base (separate collection, agent/crew two levels).
  Memory is the unified cross-task record store. The two share vector storage but serve different purposes.
axes.permissions:
**Guardrails are "task output validation", not a permission boundary — this differs from the old judgment.**

Official `concepts/tasks` page "Task Guardrails" wording:

**Official wording**: "validate and transform task outputs before they are passed to the next task"

Two implementation styles:

- **functional** — pass a `guardrail=` callback returning `(bool, result)`, deterministic validation
- **LLM-style** — pass a string description; an `LLMGuardrail` is auto-built, judged by the task's agent's LLM
- **related fields** — `guardrail` / `guardrails` / `guardrail_max_retries` (**default 3**)

**Key judgment: it only gates outputs** (task products), **not** two-way validation, and it **does not change state**:

- **not** the OpenAI Agents SDK style of input + output two-way validation
- **not** ADK's Tool Confirmation pre-execution check
- **not** LangGraph's interrupts changing state

So in the comparison table CrewAI should read "validates task outputs, retries on failure".

**Sandbox: OSS has no process / container-level sandbox.** The boundary comes from the tools themselves —
file tools restrict paths to `base_dir` by default. Default is cwd, see the local_files axis.
MCP security is officially stated as a matter of "trust", with no built-in protection.

**Unknown: network access control has no official mechanism** (tasks page and `mcp/security` page checked).
RBAC / SSO / PII redaction belong to the AMP commercial side; the open-source version does not have them.
axes.fit:
**Fits three scenarios.**

- tasks expressible as "a team with role division" (Crews)
- needing business logic to stay in plain Python with explicit control of execution paths (Flows)
- wanting to run on local models (officially naming Ollama / LM Studio); needing MCP and A2A integration; Python stacks

**Does not fit three scenarios.** All on the same negative list:

- needing process / container-level sandboxing or network access control — no official mechanism;
  guardrails only validate task outputs, file tools only limit `base_dir`

- needing "working memory" and "cross-session long-term memory" managed separately — CrewAI has unified them into one Memory class,
  no longer typed, the opposite of LangGraph's typed route

- needing a vendor-hosted true background — pure library; deploy it yourself to your own servers / VPC

sections.双抽象是它最好用的一张对照轴:
The first two Key Features in the README are exactly this contrast:

| Official sentence | Abstraction | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Crews for autonomy**: Model teams of specialized AI agents with **roles, goals, tools, and tasks** | roles/goals/tasks | collaboration needing flexible decision-making |
| **Flows for control**: Build event-driven workflows with **state, branching, routing** | events/state/branching/routing | needing precise control of execution paths |

The FAQ states the division of labor even more plainly:

> Crews provide **autonomous agent collaboration**, ideal for tasks requiring flexible
> decision-making and dynamic interaction. Flows offer **precise, event-driven control**,
> ideal for managing detailed execution paths and **secure state management**.
> You can seamlessly combine both.

**This passage is the single most useful sentence in this site's orchestration family** — "flexible use Crew, precise use Flow, mix freely"
helps people decide better than any "what framework is it" answer.
sections.状态：Flow 的 state management 是显式且结构化的:
The README example code (the `Using Crews and Flows Together` section) makes state a Pydantic model:

```python
class MarketState(BaseModel):
    ...

class AdvancedAnalysisFlow(Flow[MarketState]):
    def run(self):
        self.state.sentiment = "analyzing"
        if self.state.confidence > 0.8:
            ...
        elif self.state.confidence > 0.5:
            ...
```

**This is the "state" this site looks for** — explicit, structured, branchable on numeric thresholds.

**Persistence and cross-process recovery verified this round** (official `concepts/checkpointing`, `concepts/flows` pages).
The README writes checkpointing as **add-on as needed**. Both quotes carry the qualifier:

- "Add tools, memory, **checkpointing**, and async execution **as your system grows**"
- "Add deterministic steps, human input, structured outputs, and **checkpointing as your system grows**"

That is README positioning language; **the mechanism itself is documented in detail officially**:

- **checkpoint granularity**: event-driven, default `on_events=["task_completed"]`, i.e. **one checkpoint per completed task**.
- **persistence backends**: `JsonProvider` (one file per checkpoint, default) or `SqliteProvider` (single DB, WAL enabled).
- **cross-process recovery**: restorable from `./.checkpoints/` or the SQLite DB; Flow additionally has `@persist`
  (default `SQLiteFlowPersistence`), `kickoff(inputs={"id": ...})` resumes,
  `restore_from_state_id=` forks.

- **CLI**: `crewai checkpoint` provides a resume / fork TUI.

**This forms the most worth-watching contrast pair in this site's orchestration family with [LangGraph](./langgraph.md)**:

| | LangGraph | CrewAI |
|---|---|---|
| state persistence | ✅ **persists at every superstep** (official wording: save graph state at every superstep) | ✅ persists per completed task (event-driven, default `task_completed`) |
| persistence granularity | superstep (one graph step) | task (or custom events, e.g. `method_execution_finished`) |
| persistence backends | separate subpackages (SQLite / Postgres) | `JsonProvider` / `SqliteProvider`; Flow uses `SQLiteFlowPersistence` |
| cross-process recovery | officially promises "resuming from exactly where they left off" | restore / fork from checkpoints, CLI can resume |

sections.商业线：Crew Control Plane（AMP）要分清:
The README has a standalone Crew Control Plane Key Features section; all seven items are commercial-product features:

- Tracing & Observability (live metrics, logs, traces)
- Unified Control Plane (centralized management and scaling)
- Seamless Integrations (enterprise system integration)
- **Advanced Security** (official wording: "Built-in robust security and compliance measures")
- 24/7 Support (dedicated enterprise support)
- **On-premise and Cloud Deployment Options** (CrewAI AMP's two deployment forms)

**Note the "Advanced Security" item** —
if one of your reasons for using CrewAI is permission boundaries, **the open-source version does not have this item**.

### AMP tiers: the official page has only two tiers, and that itself is a pitfall

Verified on the official pricing page 2026-10-01: **only two tiers** (quotes not stored per the D9 rule; see the official page):

| Tier | Executions | Seats |
|---|---|---|
| **Basic** (free tier) | **50/month, the cap is 50** | 1 |
| **Enterprise** (custom) | "Sized to workflow" + Flexible overage | unlimited |

**Basic includes**:

- Visual editor + AI copilot, GitHub integration, **Export as MCP server**, Export as UI component
- Guardrails, Human-in-the-loop input, Cron scheduling
- Tracing, OpenTelemetry, LLM testing, AI agent training
- Usage dashboard, Token count, auto-scaling, community support

**Unlocked only by Enterprise**:

- SSO (MS Entra / Okta), RBAC, workload identity, PII redaction, policies
- enterprise connectors, dedicated VPC / NAT, dedicated support
- Slack/Teams support, on-site support and training, deployment and onboarding, monthly development hours

Enterprise onboarding takes **45 days**; forward deployed engineering and training are **purchased separately as needed**.

**Three conclusions that must be read out**:

**Conclusion one: Basic has no self-serve add-on path.**

Basic's add-on column reads "—".
In the official comparison table the Basic row reads **"Maximum executions = 50", "Additional executions = —"**.
**Beyond 50/month, the self-serve way out is basically only negotiating with Enterprise.**

**Conclusion two: deployment form is genuinely delivered on the commercial side.**

Enterprise explicitly supports deploying on CrewAI cloud. It also supports your own VPC / your own infrastructure.
This also delivers the README's original line:

    > On-premise and Cloud Deployment Options
**The official page also contains no forced-online-authorization wording.**

**Conclusion three: third-party quote sites are untrustworthy.**

During verification, several third-party sources gave tiers and quotes that **do not exist on the official pricing page at all**
(one source itself notes "that tier comes from a third-party aggregator, not on the official page").
**This site collects only facts readable on official pages** — per the D9 rule, this site does not even store official quotes, only links to the official page.

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs.

The test protocol is at [protocols/framework/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/framework/_protocol.md).

**Suggested measurement** (tailored to the orchestration-framework + role-abstraction dimensions):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | Implementing the same requirement with Crew vs Flow — how much code volume and readability differ | verifies whether the dual abstraction really has distinct uses |
| 2 | Attach a local quantized model via Ollama and run a full Crew | officially named as supported; real feasibility deserves verification |
| 3 | **Guardrails in practice**: LLM-style misjudgment rate, whether 3 retries suffice | mechanism known (output validation); misjudgment rate needs measurement |
| 4 | Checkpointing in practice: does resume after interruption really skip completed tasks | the official docs describe the mechanism; real behavior needs verifying |
| 5 | Overhead of passing information between Crew members (the token cost of role-playing) | role collaboration usually eats tokens; needs measuring |
| 6 | Real success rate of Flow state cross-process recovery after a crash | compare against LangGraph's superstep persistence |

related: **Orchestration-family contrast**: both do graph/flow orchestration; ADK uses Workflow Runtime nodes and routing, CrewAI uses the Crew (role collaboration) + Flow (event-driven) dual abstraction. CrewAI additionally gives MCP/A2A support.

**State-persistence route contrast**: LangGraph persists at every superstep; CrewAI is event-driven, persisting per completed task by default, with Json/Sqlite backends, resumable/forkable. Both routes now have explicit official mechanisms.
Both on the "quick start" side, but different abstractions: Deep Agents is a batteries-included harness; CrewAI is an orchestration framework with the Crew/Flow dual abstraction.
The negative contrast: that one is single-agent primitives + input/output two-way guardrails; CrewAI's guardrail validates task outputs only (and has no sandbox).
